answer: An instrumentation threat appears when the way an outcome is measured changes at the same time as an intervention, so a shift in measurement is mistaken for real improvement. The tutorial poses the question of whether the ruler changed rather than the thing measured: a county launched a Diabetes Wellness Program in January 2023 while all clinics upgraded to a new electronic health record that documented visits more thoroughly. Because the new system recoded encounters previously logged as general check-ups, recorded diabetes care visits rose even where measurement, not care, had improved.

faqs.q: What is an instrumentation threat to validity?
faqs.a: It is the risk that a change in measurement, such as new diagnostic criteria, reporting systems, or definitions, produces an apparent trend that is an artifact. The tutorial frames it as asking whether the ruler changed, not the thing being measured.

faqs.q: How can a new electronic health record create a false improvement?
faqs.a: A better documentation system can capture and recode visits that were previously logged differently, so recorded diabetes care visits increase without any change in actual care. The tutorial's new EHR moved general check-ups into the diabetes care category.

faqs.q: How can an instrumentation threat be detected?
faqs.a: Comparing against a county that adopted the same measurement change but not the program isolates the artifact. In the tutorial, County B received the new EHR alone and showed nearly the same increase as the program county, pointing to measurement rather than the program.
